analysis.one_liner: Gives domestic oil and gas producers new tax credits, depletion breaks, and faster drilling write-offs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 1995 and died there when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new tax credit — $3 per barrel of oil and 50 cents per thousand cubic feet of gas — for production from new wells and low-output "marginal" wells, phasing out as prices rise [S2] [S3]. It would also loosen the deduction for percentage depletion by repealing the limit tied to net income, expand which marginal wells qualify, and let producers immediately write off exploration costs and use more tax credits against the minimum tax [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic oil and gas producers, especially operators of marginal (stripper) wells and companies drilling new wells, would gain new credits, larger depletion deductions, and faster write-offs of drilling and exploration costs [S2] [S3]. Because the credit can be claimed against the minimum tax and the net-income limit on depletion is repealed, the benefit reaches producers even when their properties are unprofitable on paper [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a production credit of $3 per barrel of crude oil and 50 cents per thousand cubic feet of natural gas from new wells and marginal wells, phased down as prices rise above $14 per barrel [S2] [S3].

Repeals the taxable-income limit on percentage depletion for oil and gas and makes all marginal production eligible at a rate up to 25%, so producers can deduct more than their actual income from a property [S2] [S3].

Allows immediate expensing of geological and geophysical exploration costs and expands the enhanced oil recovery credit to secondary recovery methods, with both credits usable against the minimum tax [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear the cost through forgone revenue, since the credits and expanded deductions reduce income tax and minimum tax collections. Any subsidy that keeps high-cost marginal wells producing also marginally tilts energy markets toward domestic production at taxpayer expense.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the net income limitation on percentage depletion allows producers to deduct a fixed percentage of gross revenue even when a property produces no net income — a structure long criticized as a tax shelter that costs the Treasury revenue [S3].

The credits are designed to support marginal wells producing 25 barrel-equivalents a day or less, some of which are 95% water; subsidizing such wells can keep uneconomic operations running rather than letting market prices govern production [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted tax break for one industry, structured to deliver benefits even to marginal, barely-profitable wells, and paid for by the Treasury. Supporters would argue it preserves domestic production and rural oilfield jobs; the cost is forgone federal revenue with no offsetting revenue source in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 1995, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Sen. James Inhofe introduced S. 447 on February 16, 1995, with Sen. Don Nickles, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5] [S3].
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].
The action history shows no activity after the referral to Finance — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers are better off that the bill died, since it would have shifted tax burdens toward the general public to subsidize oil and gas producers. Domestic producers, particularly marginal-well operators, lost the chance at new credits and deductions.

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Don Nickles
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after the referral — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all six senators associated with the bill were Republicans, but no opposition or support beyond that is recorded.

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is new tax benefits for this industry — a per-barrel production credit, expanded depletion deductions, and faster write-offs — funded by federal taxpayers. Its gain comes at the public's expense through forgone revenue.

The credit and expanded depletion rates are aimed squarely at low-output wells, which are often unprofitable without support. Operators would gain, though the subsidy can prop up wells the market would otherwise shut down.
